passage: Teacher's note, Class 6. In the games period Mridul was told by the referee that his goal was offside and would not count. Eshaan, our PT teacher, watched him say, "Okay," with clenched jaw and pressed lips, then turn and walk away, hands in fists. He did not shout or argue, which I'd like to praise. When the game ended, though, he kicked the ball hard against the wall. I took him aside and said, "I saw you keep calm and it looked hard." He said, "It wasn't fair." We talked, and he ran two laps to burn off the energy. I will follow up on how he feels about the offside rule. — Eshaan

qa.q: What did the referee say about Mridul's goal?
qa.a: The referee said the goal was offside and would not count.

qa.q: What did Mridul's clenched jaw and fists suggest he was feeling despite saying okay?
qa.a: They suggest he was angry about what felt unfair, though he held it in. Kicking the ball later shows the anger needed a way out.

qa.q: What could Eshaan do to help Mridul with anger after being polite?
qa.a: Give a safe outlet, like the laps, listen to his view, and explain the rule calmly.

qa.q: How might the referee see Mridul's reaction?
qa.a: The referee probably saw a player who accepted the decision politely and may not have noticed how angry Mridul felt.

grounding: A child says okay while angry at a rule that feels unfair; politeness shows self-control but the anger still needs a safe outlet.

passage: Thursday night. Vikas said we couldn't play cricket in the lane because the ball hit a window last week. I said, "Okay," and smiled a small smile, and went home. But inside I was fuming. It wasn't me who broke the window! Everyone else was playing too. I banged my bag on the table and Amma raised her eyebrows. I said, "I'm fine." Later I punched my pillow ten times until I felt better. Then I told Amma what happened. She said I could ask Vikas whether we can play in the park. I think I'll do that tomorrow. — Sunaina

qa.q: Who told Sunaina they couldn't play in the lane?
qa.a: Vikas told Sunaina they couldn't play cricket in the lane.

qa.q: What did Sunaina feel when she said "Okay" with a small smile, and what did she do with the feeling later?
qa.a: Sunaina was angry because it seemed unfair, since Sunaina wasn't the one who broke the window. Sunaina let it out safely by punching her pillow and then talking to Amma.

qa.q: What could Sunaina do next about the cricket rule?
qa.a: Sunaina could ask Vikas calmly whether they can play in the park, as Amma suggested.

qa.q: How might Vikas see Sunaina's reply?
qa.a: Vikas heard an okay and a smile, so Vikas may think Sunaina accepted it and not know how Sunaina felt.

grounding: A child says okay politely while angry at a rule that feels unfair, and the anger needs a safe outlet afterwards.

passage:
In the Kerala village, Joseph was about to ride the new cycle Appachan had bought for the family. But Uncle said, "Suraj goes first. He's older."
Joseph's face tightened. He said, "Okay," through pressed lips.
Suraj rode off, grinning.
Joseph walked to the river bank and threw stones into the water, one after the other, as hard as he could. After a while, his shoulders relaxed.
Ammachi came out and sat beside him. "It's not fair, is it?"
Joseph shook his head. "I was here first."
"I'll talk to Uncle. Tomorrow, you go first."
Joseph nodded and threw one more stone, gently this time.

qa.q: Where did Joseph go to throw stones?
qa.a: To the river bank.

qa.q: What was Joseph feeling when he said "Okay" through pressed lips?
qa.a: Joseph felt angry and treated unfairly, but held it in politely.

qa.q: What helped Joseph with his anger?
qa.a: Throwing stones at the river gave him a safe outlet, and Ammachi listened and helped fix the unfairness.

qa.q: How might Suraj see the situation?
qa.a: Suraj was probably just happy to ride first, not noticing Joseph's anger.

grounding: In a village, a child says okay politely while angry at an unfair rule, then finds a safe outlet.

passage:
At football practice in Toronto, Coach Daniel told Tariq to sit out the match. "Let others have a chance."
But Tariq hadn't missed a practice all season. He said, "Okay, Coach," through tight lips.
He sat on the bench, arms crossed, jaw clenched.
After practice, he ran three laps around the field until he was out of breath. Then he found his father in the car park.
"Coach benched me for no reason," Tariq said.
His father listened. "That sounds unfair. You were polite, and that's good. Let's talk to Coach together tomorrow."
Tariq nodded. His shoulders dropped a little.

qa.q: How many laps did Tariq run after practice?
qa.a: Three laps.

qa.q: What was Tariq feeling when he said "Okay, Coach"?
qa.a: Tariq felt angry and treated unfairly, but controlled it and stayed polite.

qa.q: What did Tariq's father do that helped?
qa.a: He listened, said it sounded unfair, praised Tariq's politeness, and offered to talk to the coach together.

qa.q: How might Coach Daniel see Tariq's tight-lipped "Okay"?
qa.a: The coach might think Tariq accepted the decision, not realising how angry he felt.

grounding: A child speaks politely while angry at being benched, then releases it through running and talking to a parent.

passage:
In the Class 6 project presentation, Farida's group had worked hard on the poster. But when the teacher praised it, she said, "Well done, Tanvir! Great work!"
Farida had drawn most of the poster. She said, "Okay, Ma'am," but her voice was tight.
After class, she went to the girls' washroom and splashed water on her face. Then she wrote in her notebook, "NOT FAIR!" in big letters.
At lunch, she calmly went to the teacher. "Ma'am, I drew most of the poster. Could you please mention the whole group next time?"
The teacher paused. "I'm sorry, Farida. You're right. I'll fix it tomorrow."
Farida smiled, relieved.

qa.q: What did Farida write in her notebook?
qa.a: "NOT FAIR!" in big letters.

qa.q: What was Farida feeling when she said "Okay, Ma'am"?
qa.a: Farida felt angry and treated unfairly, but controlled it and stayed polite.

qa.q: What helped Farida handle her anger?
qa.a: Splashing water, writing in her notebook, and then calmly telling the teacher helped her release and address the anger.

qa.q: How might Tanvir feel about the teacher's praise?
qa.a: Tanvir might have felt pleased but also awkward, knowing Farida did most of the work.

grounding: A child says okay politely while angry about unfair credit, then finds safe outlets and speaks up calmly.

passage: I'm Indu, and I was in the playground when the PE teacher announced that only Class 7 could use the new football at lunch. Vaibhav had been waiting all week for that ball. He said, "Okay, Sir," but his lips were pressed thin and his ears had gone red. He didn't argue. I can't be sure what he was thinking, but he walked off very stiffly. Behind the canteen he kicked the old ball against the wall, hard, again and again, until he was out of breath. Then he sat down next to me and said, "It's not fair. We're good players too." I said maybe he could ask Sir about taking turns. The next day he did, politely, and Sir agreed to Class 6 on Fridays.

qa.q: Which class could use the new football at lunch?
qa.a: Only Class 7.

qa.q: What might Vaibhav's thin lips and red ears suggest?
qa.a: He was probably angry and disappointed at a rule that felt unfair, even while staying polite, though Indu can't be sure.

qa.q: What gave Vaibhav's anger a safe outlet?
qa.a: Kicking the old ball against the wall behind the canteen, talking it over with Indu, and the next day raising the fairness politely.

qa.q: How might the PE teacher have seen Vaibhav's "Okay, Sir"?
qa.a: The teacher might have thought Vaibhav accepted the rule calmly, missing the anger underneath until the polite request the next day.

grounding: It illustrates a school-age child saying okay through tight lips at an unfair rule, and the anger finding a safe outlet afterwards, seen by a classmate.
